subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes a direct tax from an indirect tax?

options.A: A direct tax is imposed directly on the taxpayer and cannot be shifted to someone else, whereas an indirect tax can be shifted by the taxpayer to another person, with its incidence ultimately borne by the consumer
options.B: A direct tax can always be shifted to another person, whereas an indirect tax can never be shifted
options.C: Both direct and indirect taxes are levied only on income and never on consumption or expenditure
options.D: A direct tax is levied only on companies, whereas an indirect tax is levied only on individuals

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) A direct tax is imposed directly on the taxpayer and cannot be shifted to someone else, whereas an indirect tax can be shifted by the taxpayer to another person, with its incidence ultimately borne by the consumer

A direct tax is imposed directly on the taxpayer and paid directly to the Government by the person on whom it is imposed, and cannot be shifted; income tax is a significant example. An indirect tax, by contrast, can be shifted by the taxpayer to someone else, with its incidence ultimately borne by the consumer, while the immediate liability to pay may fall on a manufacturer, service provider or seller.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Indirect taxes are described in the chapter as "regressive in nature" because:

options.B: They are not based on the principle of ability to pay, so all consumers, including the economically challenged, bear the brunt of indirect taxes equally
options.A: They are levied only on the wealthiest sections of society, in inverse proportion to income
options.C: They automatically reduce in rate as a consumer's income increases
options.D: They are levied only on luxury goods and never on essential goods or services

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) They are not based on the principle of ability to pay, so all consumers, including the economically challenged, bear the brunt of indirect taxes equally

Indirect taxes, also called consumption taxes, are regressive in nature because they are not based on the principle of ability to pay; all consumers, including the economically challenged, bear the brunt of indirect taxes equally, since such taxes are levied on consumption, expenditure, privilege or right, and not on income or property.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: "Tax cascading", as explained in the chapter, refers to:

options.C: Tax on tax - a situation avoided under GST since only the value added at each stage is taxed
options.A: A situation where tax rates increase progressively at each stage of the supply chain by a fixed percentage
options.B: A method of calculating customs duty on imported goods based on their assessable value
options.D: A scheme under which small taxpayers pay tax at a fixed, lower composition rate

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Tax on tax - a situation avoided under GST since only the value added at each stage is taxed

Tax cascading means tax on tax. Since only the value added at each stage is taxed under GST (through the continuous chain of input tax credit), there is no tax on tax or cascading of taxes under the GST system, unlike under the earlier fragmented indirect tax regime.

question_html: GST is described as a "destination-based" consumption tax because:

options.A: The GST revenue goes to the State/Union Territory where the goods or services are ultimately consumed, not where they are manufactured or produced
options.B: The GST revenue goes to the State/Union Territory where the goods or services are manufactured or produced, not where they are consumed
options.C: GST revenue is divided equally among all States regardless of where consumption or production occurs
options.D: GST is levied only at the final retail point of sale, with no tax collected at any earlier stage

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The GST revenue goes to the State/Union Territory where the goods or services are ultimately consumed, not where they are manufactured or produced

GST is a destination-based consumption tax levied on the supply of goods or services; the GST revenue goes to the State/Union Territory where the goods or services are ultimately consumed, as opposed to the earlier origin-based indirect tax regime (like VAT/CST) where tax largely went to the producing/selling State.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: "Continuous chain of tax credits" under GST means:

options.C: Credit of tax paid on inward supplies is available for payment of tax on outward supplies, with the supplier at each stage permitted to set off this credit against the GST payable on his own outward supply
options.A: Credit accumulated by one taxpayer can be transferred and used by any other unrelated taxpayer in the supply chain
options.B: Credit is available only to the very first supplier in the supply chain and lapses thereafter
options.D: Credit of tax paid can be carried forward indefinitely but never actually utilised against any tax liability

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Credit of tax paid on inward supplies is available for payment of tax on outward supplies, with the supplier at each stage permitted to set off this credit against the GST payable on his own outward supply

Continuous chain of tax credits means that credit of tax paid on inward supplies is available for payment of tax on outward supplies; the supplier at each stage is permitted to avail credit of GST paid on purchase of goods and/or services and set off this credit against the GST payable on his own outward supply, so that only the final consumer bears the GST charged by the last supplier.

question_html: Why could CENVAT and State-Level VAT credits not be set off against each other under the earlier regime, despite both being value added taxes?

options.B: Because CENVAT was a Central levy and State-Level VAT was a State levy, so set-off of one against the credit of the other was not possible
options.A: Because CENVAT applied only to services while State-Level VAT applied only to goods
options.C: Because CENVAT and State-Level VAT were levied at identical rates, making any set-off unnecessary
options.D: Because State-Level VAT was abolished before CENVAT was introduced, so no overlap ever existed

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Because CENVAT was a Central levy and State-Level VAT was a State levy, so set-off of one against the credit of the other was not possible

Though CENVAT and State-Level VAT were essentially value added taxes, set-off of one against the credit of another was not possible because CENVAT was a Central levy and State-Level VAT was a State levy; this non-integration was one of the key deficiencies that led to cascading of taxes under the earlier regime.

question_html: Under the pre-GST VAT regime, what made it extremely difficult and cumbersome for a business to operate across State borders?

options.D: Each State had its own VAT provisions, with different tax rates, registration procedures, due dates for tax payment/return filing, definitions of basic terms, methods of computing tax and lists of exemptions
options.A: Every State was legally required to adopt the exact same VAT rate, procedure and registration format, making cross-border business unusually simple

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Each State had its own VAT provisions, with different tax rates, registration procedures, due dates for tax payment/return filing, definitions of basic terms, methods of computing tax and lists of exemptions

Before the advent of GST, under the VAT regime, each State had its own VAT provisions with different tax rates, registration procedures, due dates for tax payment and return filing, definitions of basic terms, methods of computing tax and lists of exemptions; a business operating in multiple States had to comply with a completely different set of VAT provisions in each one, making cross-border business extremely difficult and cumbersome.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Under India's Concurrent Dual GST Model:

options.A: The Centre and States simultaneously levy GST on the complete supply chain, from production to distribution; the Centre also has the power to tax intra-State sales and the States are empowered to tax services
options.B: Only the Centre levies GST, with States having no power to levy any component of GST
options.C: Only the States levy GST, with the Centre having no power to levy any component of GST
options.D: GST is levied sequentially, first by the Centre and then, at a later stage of the supply chain, by the States, but never simultaneously

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The Centre and States simultaneously levy GST on the complete supply chain, from production to distribution; the Centre also has the power to tax intra-State sales and the States are empowered to tax services

India has adopted a Concurrent Dual GST Model owing to its unique federal structure; under this model, the Centre and States simultaneously levy GST on the complete supply chain, starting from production to distribution, with the Centre now empowered to tax intra-State sales and the States empowered to tax services.

question_html: Which of the following correctly identifies the components of GST in India and the authority levying/collecting each?

options.C: CGST is levied and collected by the Central Government, SGST by State Governments/Union Territories with Legislatures, and UTGST by Union Territories without Legislatures, on intra-State supplies, while IGST is levied by the Centre on inter-State supplies
options.A: CGST, SGST and UTGST are all levied and collected exclusively by the Central Government, with States having no role at all
options.B: IGST is levied jointly by every State Government together, with the Centre having no role in its levy
options.D: SGST is levied by the Central Government while CGST is levied by the respective State Governments

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) CGST is levied and collected by the Central Government, SGST by State Governments/Union Territories with Legislatures, and UTGST by Union Territories without Legislatures, on intra-State supplies, while IGST is levied by the Centre on inter-State supplies

GST in India comprises CGST (levied and collected by the Central Government), SGST (levied and collected by State Governments/Union Territories with Legislatures) and UTGST (levied and collected by Union Territories without Legislatures), all on intra-State supplies; inter-State supplies are subject to IGST, levied by the Centre.

question_html: IGST is best described as:

options.D: The sum total of CGST and SGST/UTGST, levied by the Centre on all inter-State supplies
options.A: A tax entirely separate from and unrelated to CGST and SGST/UTGST, levied only on imports
options.B: A reduced-rate tax applicable only to supplies made by composition taxpayers
options.C: A tax levied exclusively by State Governments on inter-State supplies

IGST is the sum total of CGST and SGST/UTGST and is levied by the Centre on all inter-State supplies; this ensures that the combined tax burden on an inter-State supply mirrors that on a comparable intra-State supply, which is levied as CGST plus SGST/UTGST.

question_html: As a general rule, a supply of goods or services is treated as an "intra-State supply" when:

options.A: The location of the supplier and the place of supply of goods or services are in the same State/Union Territory
options.B: The location of the supplier and the place of supply are in two different States

question_html: How does GST mitigate the ill effects of cascading, benefiting trade and industry?

options.D: By providing a comprehensive input tax credit mechanism across the entire supply chain, eradicating tax on tax and allowing cross-utilisation of input tax credits, making the entire supply chain tax neutral
options.A: By levying tax only once, at the point of manufacture, with no tax at any subsequent stage of the supply chain
options.B: By allowing every trader to independently decide whether or not to remit collected tax to the Government

Correct answer: (D) By providing a comprehensive input tax credit mechanism across the entire supply chain, eradicating tax on tax and allowing cross-utilisation of input tax credits, making the entire supply chain tax neutral

GST is designed so that tax is collected at every stage, with credit of tax paid at the previous stage available to set off the tax to be paid at the next stage; this eradicates tax on tax and allows cross-utilisation of input tax credits, benefiting industry by making the entire supply chain tax neutral, mitigating the ill effects of cascading.

question_html: Why did the introduction of GST necessitate an amendment to the Constitution?

options.A: Because the Constitutional provisions had delineated separate powers for the Centre (excise duty on manufacture, service tax) and the States (VAT on sale of goods, with CST on inter-State sales collected/retained by States), and GST required amendment to enable integration of these levies and empower both Centre and States to simultaneously levy and collect a comprehensive GST
options.B: Because the Constitution, prior to amendment, gave States the exclusive power to levy all forms of indirect tax, including service tax
options.C: Because the Constitution did not permit the levy of any indirect tax whatsoever prior to the amendment
options.D: Because the amendment was required solely to rename existing taxes without any change in the underlying powers of the Centre or States

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Because the Constitutional provisions had delineated separate powers for the Centre (excise duty on manufacture, service tax) and the States (VAT on sale of goods, with CST on inter-State sales collected/retained by States), and GST required amendment to enable integration of these levies and empower both Centre and States to simultaneously levy and collect a comprehensive GST

The Constitutional provisions hitherto delineated separate powers for the Centre (excise duty on goods, exclusive power to tax services) and the States (VAT on sale of goods, entry tax, etc.), with CST on inter-State sales levied by the Centre but collected/retained by States. Introduction of GST required a constitutional amendment to enable integration of these levies into a comprehensive GST and to empower both Centre and States to simultaneously levy and collect it, resulting in the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016.

question_html: Ridhwaan Distributors holds an IGST credit of ₹10,800 (paid on its purchase from Farhaan) and must pay CGST of ₹6,480 and SGST of ₹6,480 (9% each of ₹72,000) on its supply to Chetna Retail Corner. options.A: Net CGST payable of ₹6,480 and net SGST payable of ₹6,480, since IGST credit can never be used to pay CGST or SGST
options.B: Net CGST payable of ₹2,160 and net SGST payable of Nil, since IGST credit must be applied to SGST before CGST

case_facts_html: Nandika Precision Tools, located in State P, is the first supplier of certain goods and sells them to Farhaan Industrial Traders, also located in State P, for ₹50,000, charging CGST and SGST at 9% each (Nandika has no input credit, being the first supplier). Farhaan Industrial Traders then supplies the same goods, after a 20% value addition, to Ridhwaan Distributors located in State Q - an inter-State supply - charging IGST at 18% on the value of ₹60,000. Ridhwaan Distributors, in turn, supplies the goods, after a further 20% value addition, to Chetna Retail Corner, also located in State Q - an intra-State supply - at a value of ₹72,000, charging CGST and SGST at 9% each.
question_html: Since State P did not ultimately consume the goods (they moved to State Q for consumption), how does the settlement mechanism between the States and the Centre operate in respect of the credit utilised in this chain?

options.D: State P transfers to the Centre the SGST credit of ₹4,500 that Farhaan utilised in payment of IGST, and the Centre transfers to State Q the IGST credit of ₹4,320 that Ridhwaan utilised in payment of SGST, since State Q is where the goods are actually consumed
options.A: No fund transfer is required between States and the Centre, since GST revenue is retained permanently by whichever State the supplier is located in
options.B: State Q transfers funds to State P, since State P was the State from which the goods originated
options.C: The Centre retains all revenue from inter-State transactions permanently, with no transfer to any State at any point

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) State P transfers to the Centre the SGST credit of ₹4,500 that Farhaan utilised in payment of IGST, and the Centre transfers to State Q the IGST credit of ₹4,320 that Ridhwaan utilised in payment of SGST, since State Q is where the goods are actually consumed

Since GST is a destination-based tax, SGST revenue should ultimately accrue to the consuming State; because State P's SGST credit (₹4,500) was used to pay IGST, State P transfers that amount to the Centre, and because the Centre's IGST revenue was subsequently used by Ridhwaan to pay SGST (₹4,320) in State Q - the State of actual consumption - the Centre transfers that amount to State Q, ensuring SGST revenue ultimately flows to the destination State.

One-half of the total number of Members of the GST Council constitutes the quorum. subject: Goods and Services Tax
case_facts_html: Saloni Verma runs Verma Precision Auto Components, a manufacturing business with an aggregate turnover (based on PAN) of ₹6.2 crore in FY 2024-25 and ₹7.1 crore in FY 2025-26, supplying components to customers in multiple States. She previously found the erstwhile VAT/CENVAT regime cumbersome, since she had to maintain separate registrations, rates and return formats for each State she supplied to, and could not set off her central excise duty credit against State VAT liability. Since transitioning fully to GST, she files all her returns, registration applications and refund claims online through a single common portal, and her team is now assessing whether her business must issue e-invoices for FY 2026-27.
question_html: Given that Saloni's PAN-based aggregate turnover exceeded ₹5 crore in FY 2025-26 (a preceding financial year from 2017-18 onwards), is Verma Precision Auto Components required to issue e-invoices, and through which portal are such e-invoices reported?

options.D: Yes, since its aggregate turnover (based on PAN) in a preceding financial year from 2017-18 onwards (FY 2025-26, at ₹7.1 crore) exceeds ₹5 crore, it is required to issue e-invoices, reported/uploaded through the Invoice Registration Portal (IRP), managed by the National Informatics Centre
options.A: No, since e-invoicing is determined solely by the current year's turnover, and only FY 2024-25's ₹6.2 crore is relevant, which does not exceed ₹5 crore
options.B: Yes, but e-invoices must be reported through the e-way bill portal, www.ewaybillgst.gov.in, rather than the Invoice Registration Portal
options.C: No, since e-invoicing applies only to service providers and not to manufacturers such as Verma Precision Auto Components

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Yes, since its aggregate turnover (based on PAN) in a preceding financial year from 2017-18 onwards (FY 2025-26, at ₹7.1 crore) exceeds ₹5 crore, it is required to issue e-invoices, reported/uploaded through the Invoice Registration Portal (IRP), managed by the National Informatics Centre

All registered businesses with an aggregate turnover (based on PAN) in any preceding financial year from 2017-18 onwards greater than ₹5 crore are required to issue e-invoices; since Saloni's turnover exceeded ₹5 crore in FY 2025-26 (and indeed also FY 2024-25), this threshold is met, and e-invoices are uploaded/reported through the Invoice Registration Portal (IRP), managed by the National Informatics Centre, Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology, Government of India - distinct from the e-way bill portal.
